newsitem.title: USA: Cephalon stock tumbles after FDA finds drug ineffective.
newsitem.headline: Cephalon stock tumbles after FDA finds drug ineffective.

text.p: The stock of drug maker Cephalon Inc. tumbled 40 percent Friday after a panel of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration rejected recommending approval of its drug for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or Lou Gehrig's disease.
Cephalon stock was off $8, or 40 percent, at $12 in morning trading on the Nasdaq market.
In a 6-3 decision, the FDA panel voted Thursday against recommending approval of Cephalon's Myotrophin (recombinant human insulin growth factor-1) injection for ALS, an ultimately fatal disease.
Myotrophin was the lead drug candidate for Cephalon, a development stage biotechnology company that has not yet brought any products to market.

The FDA panel said the company, which is based in West Chester, Pa., did not present substantial evidence that Myotrophin injection was effective in the treatment of ALS, which kills 10,000 Americans a year and afflicts up to 30,000.
"The data do not look robust, they look modest," the panel chairman, Dr. Sid Gilman of the University of Michigan Medical Centre, said.
The finding was in response to a New Drug Application submitted to the FDA by Cephalon and a request for approval to market the drug submitted by Chiron Corp.

"We are deeply disappointed with the committee's finding about Myotrophin Injection. We appreciate the many expressions of support from patients, caregivers and physicians and will be reviewing with the FDA the panel's recommendation," Frank Baldino, Jr., Cephalon's president and chief executive, and William Rutter, Chiron's chairman, said in a joint statement.
Chiron, which develops and markets pharmaceuticals, is based in Emeryville, Calif. Its stock was off $1.50 at $18.50 in morning trading on Nasdaq.
Shares of Cephalon and, to a lesser extent, Chiron had been volatile since last June, when Myotrophin first went before the FDA advisory panel.
A drug for ALS is already on the market. Rhone-Poulenc Rorer's Rilutek (riluzole) was approved by the FDA in 1995.

The disease, which attacks nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord, causing progressive paralysis and loss of respiratory function, gets its common name from the New York Yankees baseball great Lou Gehrig, who died of it.
ALS patients survive only about three years after diagnosis.
